characters.identity: A Gujjar man who has patrolled Mangar Bani since his father did. His family's memory of the forest spans three generations. He speaks of the ridge as kin, not resource.
characters.psychological_depth: Carries a quiet authority that comes from continuity. Suspicious of outsiders but generous once trust is established. Mourns what has been lost at the edges without melodrama.

characters.identity: A retired civil servant who has counted birds at Okhla every winter morning for twenty-two years. His notebooks are the closest thing the sanctuary has to a long-term ecological record.
characters.psychological_depth: Meticulous, patient, quietly furious at institutional indifference. Finds in bird counting a discipline that the rest of his life lacked.

characters.identity: A researcher at JNU whose work on leopard movement corridors across the Aravalli fragments has made her one of the most cited urban ecologists in India.
characters.psychological_depth: Believes in the corridor dream but has been disappointed enough times to measure hope in small increments. The science and the grief coexist in her without contradiction.

characters.identity: A mid-sized real estate developer working the Faridabad–Gurugram fringe. Not a villain — a man with his own logic, his own pressures, his own version of what the land is for.
characters.psychological_depth: Genuinely believes he is building homes for people who need them. Uncomfortable with the conversation about ecology but not dishonest.

characters.identity: A first-generation college student at JNU from a small town in Uttar Pradesh. She has never been in a forest before. The ravine outside her hostel window is the first wild thing she has had time to notice.
characters.psychological_depth: Her discovery of the forest is the reader's discovery. She asks the questions that expertise has forgotten to ask.
